query: Which module talks to the native Windows console API through ctypes so that Unicode text can be read from and written to a terminal window without going through byte-oriented standard streams?
why: Whole file is the ctypes kernel32 bridge: binds ReadConsoleW/WriteConsoleW/GetConsoleMode (L44-46), raw IO base/reader/writer classes (L119-192), ConsoleStream wrapper (L195), text stdin/stdout/stderr factories (L227-260), console detection and stream selection (L264-end). _compat.py only dispatches to it.

query: Which module keeps a per-thread stack of the active invocation contexts so that helper code anywhere can look up the current one without having it passed in explicitly?
why: Entire 68-line file is the thread-local context stack: threading.local store (L9), lookup of the top of the stack with silent/raise modes (L12-41), push/pop (L44-51), and a color-default helper that reads the current context (L54-67). core.py only calls push/pop.

query: Where are the tests making sure that captured stdout and stderr buffers in the in-process command runner stay open and correct across garbage collection, active logging handlers, worker threads and many back-to-back invocations?
why: Module docstring (L1-38) states its scope; six categories: wrapper must not close buffers (L57-105), mixer lifecycle/GC (L108-181), logging interaction (L184-289), multi-threaded safety (L292-366), sequential invocation isolation (L369-480), stress reproducers (L483-540).

query: Where are the tests showing that a context-wide token transform (such as lowercasing) lets users type option names, choice values and subcommand names in any letter case?
why: Whole file sets a lowercasing token_normalize_func in CONTEXT_SETTINGS (L3) and tests it for option names (L6-15), Choice values (L18-50) and group subcommand names (L53-63). No other test file uses token_normalize_func.

query: Which example program strings several subcommands together on one command line so that each step feeds its output into the next, loading, transforming and saving pictures like a unix pipe?
why: Chained group with pipe docstring (L10-20), result callback that pipes processors (L23-39), processor/generator decorators (L42-66), and eleven image steps open/save/display/resize/crop/transpose/blur/smoothen/emboss/sharpen/paste (L74-end) using PIL.

query: Which module absorbs the differences in how text and binary standard streams, ANSI-code detection, and safe atomic file writes behave across operating systems and Python stream implementations, so the rest of the codebase can call one consistent set of stream helpers?
why: Whole file (626 lines) is the platform/stream compatibility layer: text-stream wrapping and encoding detection (19-53), a non-closing text wrapper and stream fixups (56-151), binary/text reader-writer detection (151-316), the binary/text stdin/stdout/stderr accessors (316-357), open_stream plus the _AtomicFile temp-then-rename writer (358-486), and ANSI stripping/tty detection helpers (488-583).

query: Which module holds the concrete mechanics behind several interactive terminal features at once: a progress meter that estimates time remaining, several backend strategies for paging long output through an external program, spawning an editor and detecting whether the user actually saved, and opening a URL or file with the platform's default handler?
why: 945-line file: ProgressBar with eta/rendering (57-388), pager selection and three backend strategies - pipe, tempfile, null (400-655), Editor spawning and save detection (656-770), open_url with per-OS launchers (772-840), and platform-specific raw_terminal/getchar implementations at the end (842-945).

query: Which module recomputes the standard library's line-breaking algorithm so that where a line must break, or a single overlong token must be cut, is decided by on-screen character count instead of raw string length, treating embedded terminal escape codes as contributing no width at all?
why: Whole 189-line file: _truncate_visible walks a string counting only non-escape-sequence characters toward its budget (11-35), and TextWrapper overrides _handle_long_word (48-64) and _wrap_chunks (66-162) to route every width measurement through that visible-length counting instead of len(); extra_indent and indent_only round out the class.

query: Where are the tests confirming that a command group can be told to build its context, its own command object, and the subcommands and sub-groups it creates out of caller-supplied replacement classes instead of the library's built-in ones, including a group class that produces more instances of itself?
why: Whole short file: test_command_context_class (4), test_context_invoke_type (20), test_context_formatter_class (47), test_group_command_class (66), test_group_group_class (84) and test_group_group_class_self (102) each swap in a custom cls= for context/command/formatter/group and check it was used.

query: Which example command group looks up user-typed shorthand names in a config file in place of the real subcommand names, and, failing that, accepts any truncated prefix of a subcommand name as long as it matches exactly one candidate?
why: Whole file: Config reads/writes a shorthand-name mapping from an ini file (7-31); the custom group's get_command first checks that mapping, then falls back to case-insensitive prefix matching among list_commands, failing loudly on more than one match (42-68); resolve_command is overridden so the resolved command's real name is reported, not the shorthand typed (70-73).

query: Which example CLI discovers its own subcommands by scanning a directory for files that follow a naming convention and importing each one on demand, rather than registering every subcommand up front in the source?
why: Whole file: ComplexCLI.list_commands scans cmd_folder for files starting with 'cmd_' and strips the prefix/suffix to get command names (32-38); get_command does a dynamic __import__ of complex.commands.cmd_<name> and returns its cli object, returning nothing if the module doesn't exist (40-45).

query: Which example shows the same kind of parameter check implemented three different ways in one program: as a reusable callback function, as a custom type's conversion method, and as an inline check written directly in the command body?
why: Whole file: validate_count is a callback rejecting negative or odd values (6-9); the URL class's convert method rejects non-http(s) schemes (12-22); and the cli() function body itself rejects a --foo value other than the one allowed string (40-45) - three validation sites for the same command.

query: Where are the tests that drive the completion-suggestion machinery end to end against many different kinds of command-line objects - plain commands, groups, choices, file and path parameters - to check what gets suggested at each point in a partially typed command line?
why: Helper functions _get_completions/_get_words (22-28) wrap ShellComplete.get_completions and are reused across the file's tests against Command, Group, Argument, Option, Choice, File and Path objects to assert which completion values come back for a given partial input.

query: Where are the tests that push option declaration and parsing through a wide variety of edge cases in one file - unconventional prefix characters, suggesting a close match for an unrecognized option, combining multiple values with environment-variable sourcing, boolean flags read from environment values, and old forward-slash-style option syntax?
why: Single large file covering many option edge cases: test_prefixes (21), test_suggest_possible_options (169), test_multiple_envvar (421), test_boolean_flag_envvar (519), test_winstyle_options and test_legacy_options (829, 846) among 40+ tests exercising the option-parsing machinery from many angles.

query: Where are the tests checking that a shared state object handed down through nested subcommands is created only when asked for and reused rather than duplicated, that its lifetime cleanup callbacks run in the right order even across nested exits, and that eager callbacks fire before ordinary ones?
why: test_ensure_context_objects/test_get_context_objects(_no_ensuring/_missing) (17-108) check create-vs-find semantics for a shared object across nested commands; test_close_before_pop/test_close_before_exit (336, 357) check cleanup callback ordering; test_multiple_eager_callbacks (395) checks eager-before-normal callback ordering.
